claims.claim: Entrepreneurship involves taking a risk, either to create a new business or to greatly change the scope and direction of an existing one (OpenStax).
Entrepreneurs are people with vision, drive, and creativity who are willing to take the risk of starting and managing a business to make a profit (OpenStax).

Many successful businesses get started because someone identifies a need and then finds a way to fill it (OpenStax); about 80 percent of Inc. 500 executives got the idea for their company while working in the same or a related industry.
Having a great concept is not enough: an entrepreneur must be able to develop and manage the company that implements the idea (OpenStax).

Most successful entrepreneurs favor business opportunities that carry a moderate degree of risk where they can better control the outcome, over highly risky ventures where luck plays a large role (OpenStax).

Although entrepreneurs may be small-business owners, not all small-business owners are entrepreneurs; entrepreneurs typically are innovators who start companies to pursue ideas for a new product or service, and growth-oriented entrepreneurs want their business to grow into a major corporation (OpenStax).
Small businesses represent about half of U.S. economic output and employ about half of the private sector workforce (OpenStax 5.3, citing SBA and Kauffman data).

Business survival rates reached a three-decade high of 48.7 percent in 2016, meaning nearly half of new businesses made it to their fifth year of operation — and roughly half did not (OpenStax reporting Kauffman Index data).
A good business plan guides you through each stage of starting and managing your business; it is a roadmap for how to structure, run, and grow the business and helps you get funding (SBA).
Market research helps you find customers for your business (SBA).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where the line falls between entrepreneur and small-business owner: sources use 'entrepreneur' loosely to cover most small-business owners in everyday speech, while the textbook reserves the term for founders who take on risk to create a new business or greatly change an existing one.
positions: 'The term entrepreneur is often used in a broad sense to include most small-business owners' (OpenStax 5.1)
'Although entrepreneurs may be small-business owners, not all small-business owners are entrepreneurs' (OpenStax 5.1)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the two as overlapping but distinct: the entrepreneur's defining act is taking risk to create a new business or greatly change an existing one, and the lesson acknowledges the loose everyday usage.

conflictingEvidence.issue: New-business survival statistics vary by source, year, and definition of 'business' (with or without employees); the widely repeated 'half fail within five years' figure depends on the dataset.
positions: Kauffman Index data as reported by OpenStax: survival to year five reached 48.7% in 2016, a three-decade high
Other datasets and years report different survival rates depending on whether employer and non-employer businesses are included
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the specific, dated figure (48.7% to year five, 2016, as reported in OpenStax) and frames the general claim as 'roughly half' rather than asserting a precise universal rate.
